rewritten_text: “As the weeks passed, I became more and more absorbed in you. Then something changed. I had drawn you as Paris in delicate armor, and as Adonis in a hunter’s cloak, carrying a shining spear for hunting boar. Wearing a crown of heavy lotus flowers, you had sat at the front of Adrian’s barge and gazed across the green, muddy Nile. You had bent over a still pool in a Greek wood and seen the beauty of your own face reflected in its silent silver water. All of it had been what art should be: free of self-consciousness, ideal, and distant. Then one day—a disastrous day, I sometimes think—I decided to paint a wonderful portrait of you as you really are. You would wear your own clothes and belong to your own time, instead of dressing in costumes from the distant past. I cannot say whether it was this realistic approach or simply the wonder of your personality, presented so directly, with nothing to hide it. But as I painted, every thin layer and trace of color seemed to reveal my secret. I became afraid that other people would discover how I worshipped you. Dorian, I felt I had said too much and put too much of myself into the picture. That was when I decided I would never let it be exhibited. You were a little annoyed, but you didn’t understand everything it meant to me. I told Harry, and he laughed. That didn’t bother me. Once the portrait was finished and I sat alone with it, I felt certain I was right.... A few days later it left my studio. As soon as I escaped the unbearable fascination of having it there, I thought I had been foolish. What did it show beyond your extraordinary good looks and my ability to paint? Even now, I cannot help thinking we are mistaken when we believe the passion we feel while creating something truly appears in the finished work. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Shape and color tell us about shape and color, nothing more. Often I feel that art hides the artist far more thoroughly than it reveals him. So when this offer came from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the main attraction of my exhibition. I never imagined that you would refuse. Now I see you were right. The picture must not be shown. Don’t be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have told you.”

“Never!” the girl replied.

“Tell me why.”

“For one reason,” she answered firmly, “that the lady knows and will support me in. I know she will, because she promised. And for another reason as well: however bad his life has been, mine has been bad too. Many of us have followed the same path together, and I won’t turn against people who could have turned against me—any of them—but never did, bad as they are.”

“Then,” the gentleman said quickly, as though he had reached the very point he wanted, “put Monks in my hands, and let me deal with him.”

“What if he turns against the others?”

“I promise that if we force the truth out of him, the matter will end there. There must be circumstances in Oliver’s short history that would be painful to expose publicly. Once the truth is established, the others will go free.”

“And if it isn’t?” the girl asked.

“Then,” the gentleman continued, “this Fagin will not be prosecuted without your consent. In that situation, I think I could give you reasons that would persuade you to agree.”

“Do I have the lady’s promise of that?” she asked.

“You do,” Rose replied. “My sincere and solemn promise.”

“Monks would never find out how you learned what you know?” the girl said after a brief pause.

“Never,” the gentleman answered. “We would use the information against him in such a way that he could never even guess.”

“I’ve been a liar and lived among liars since I was a small child,” the girl said after another silence, “but I’ll take your word for it.”

Both assured her that she could safely trust them. She then began to describe the name and location of the pub from which she had been followed that night. Her voice was so quiet that the listener often struggled to make out even the general meaning of her words. Judging by her occasional pauses, the gentleman seemed to be jotting down the information she gave him. She carefully explained the surroundings, the best place to keep watch without attracting attention, and the night and hour when Monks most often visited. Then she appeared to think for a few moments, trying to bring his face and appearance more clearly to mind.

“He’s tall,” the girl said, “and strongly built, though not fat. He walks in a sneaking way, constantly looking over his shoulder, first to one side and then the other.”

I would pretend to die. My satisfied heirs would take my wealth, and I would buy my freedom. But the plan had to be carefully devised. I could not leave myself penniless; I needed to secure some money. What degrading tricks would I be driven to? Yet the alternative was an entire life of lies. Whenever guilt at planning a deception made me recoil, a visit from some aunt or cousin inevitably drew me back and strengthened my resolve. They would tell me that everyone must die, then suggest that my father had surely lost his mind after my mother’s death. He had been mad, they said, and I was fortunate: in one of his fits, he might have killed me instead of destroying his own deranged life. Naturally, all this was delicately expressed, never in blunt language that might hurt my feelings, but

Whispered here and there, in dark hints, soft and low,

with lowered eyes and sympathetic smiles or whimpers. I listened with a calm face while every nerve shook, unable to say either yes or no to all this blasphemy. What a delightful life, so entirely free of deceit! I wore the look of a dove and carried the heart of a fox. For I felt only the humiliation of lying, without any sacred sense of my own innocence to redeem it. Once I had dressed myself in the shining garment of sincerity; now I must borrow one of many colors. At first it might fit awkwardly, but practice would teach me to arrange its folds elegantly, to lie with grace. Yes, I could stain my soul with falsehood until its natural color was completely hidden. Beloved father, accept your unhappy daughter’s pure heart. Let me join you as unstained as I once was, or you will not recognize what I have become. As grief might alter Constance, deceit would alter me, until in heaven you would say, “This is not my child.” My father, to be happy now and when we meet again, I must escape this whole life, which mocks someone like me. Only in solitude will I be myself; in solitude I will be yours.

Even now I look back with disgust on the tricks and schemes by which, after many painful struggles, I arranged my escape. I could describe at length the methods I used, first to secure a small income for the rest of my life, and then to convince everyone I was dead. I could, but I will not.
